title: Availability: serial and parallel
summary: Chain components in series and availability drops. Add redundant copies in parallel and it rises. See the numbers for your design.

verdicts.text: Copies in the same failure domain fail together, so they add almost nothing. Spread them across zones or hosts for the parallel maths to hold.
Dependencies in series multiply. Several components at the same availability give a much lower total than any one of them.
Good, but each extra serial dependency costs you.
Redundant copies in independent domains lift the whole chain.

tries: Chain 8 components at 99.9 percent with one copy each.
Add a second copy to each. The total improves a lot.
Tick the shared failure domain. The extra copies stop helping.

chart.title: Availability falls as the chain grows

title: On-call load
summary: Pages, handling time and team size decide whether on-call is sustainable. See pages per shift, time spent and the load on each person.

readouts.label: Hours handling pages in an on-call week
Night pages in an on-call week

verdicts.text: More than about two incidents per shift leaves no time to fix causes and people burn out. Reduce pages at the source before adding people.
A small rotation means being on call too often, and any absence is felt.
Many pages wake people at night. Move non-urgent alerts to tickets.
A sustainable load.

tries: Set 8 pages a day.
Lower night pages by turning noisy alerts into tickets.
Shrink the team to 3 and watch the frequency.

title: Capacity runway
summary: Usage grows each month and new capacity takes time to arrive. See how many months you have and whether you order early enough.

nodes.label: Runway
nodes.sub: fmt(max(0, months), 1) + " months to the ceiling"

readouts.label: Months of spare time after lead time

verdicts.text: You are already above the safe ceiling.
Capacity takes longer to arrive than you have left. You will hit the ceiling first. Order now, or shed load.
Almost no slack. Any delay in delivery causes a shortage.
There is time to order before the ceiling.

tries: Set 8 percent growth with a 6 month lead time.
Lower the ceiling and see the runway shrink.
Remember that growth compounds.

title: Where incident time goes
summary: An outage is the sum of detecting, responding, diagnosing and fixing. See which stage to improve and what that does to a year of availability.
vars: dg >= max(detect, ack, fx) ? "diagnosing" : (fx >= max(detect, ack) ? "mitigating" : (detect >= ack ? "detecting" : "responding"))

verdicts.text: Under three nines. Look at the biggest stage first. Shaving the longest stage is worth more than polishing a short one.
Reasonable, but there is room. Runbooks and quick rollback cut diagnosis and fixing the most.
Quick detection and recovery keep the year well within a high target.

tries: Set diagnosis to 120 minutes.
Turn on runbooks and rollback. Both long stages halve.
Cut incidents per year and compare with cutting time per incident.

title: NAT port exhaustion
summary: Many clients share a few public addresses. See when connections to one destination run out of source ports and new connections fail.

inputs.label: Concurrent connections to one destination per client
Usable ports per address and destination

verdicts.text: Not enough source ports for this destination. New connections time out or reset while old ones are open. Add addresses, reuse connections, or spread across destinations.
Close to exhaustion. A traffic spike or slow-closing connections tips it over.
Plenty of ports.

tries: Raise clients to 2000.
Add public addresses to the gateway.
Reduce connections per client with keep-alive and pooling.

title: Horizontal pod autoscaling
summary: The autoscaler adds pods when utilisation passes a target. See how many pods you need, and what happens when the maximum is too low.

verdicts.text: The maximum is too low. All pods are past their capacity, so requests queue and fail. Raise the maximum or reduce load per request.
Pods run hot. Scale-up takes time, so a spike now would hurt.
The minimum keeps more pods than needed, which costs money but gives headroom.
Pods follow the load and stay under the target.

tries: Raise requests to 5000 with a maximum of 10.
Raise the maximum.
Lower the target for more headroom, at higher cost.

title: Liveness probes under load
summary: Under heavy load responses slow down. If the liveness probe times out, healthy pods are killed and the rest get more load. See when that cascade starts.

inputs.label: Use readiness for slowness, liveness for deadlocks only

nodes.label: Pods
nodes.sub: left + " of " + pods + " left, x" + fmt(extra, 1) + " load each"

verdicts.text: Slow answers fail the liveness probe, so Kubernetes kills busy but healthy pods. The rest take more load, slow down and fail too. A small overload becomes an outage.
A readiness probe takes slow pods out of rotation without restarting them, so they can recover.
Responses stay inside the probe timeout.

tries: Raise the latency above the timeout with readiness mode off.
Switch to readiness for slowness.
Lengthen the timeout and see the margin.

title: Requests and scheduling
summary: The scheduler places pods by what they request, not what they use. See how inflated requests leave pods pending on a mostly idle cluster.

verdicts.text: Pods are pending while the cluster sits mostly idle. Requests are far above real use. Right-size requests from measured usage.
Some pods cannot be placed. Add nodes or reduce requests.
Pods use more than they request, so nodes can be overcommitted and throttled or evicted.
Everything is scheduled.

tries: Request 2 cores per pod while using 0.3.
Lower the request toward real use.
Raise real use above the request and see the risk.

chart.title: Pods that fit against request size

title: etcd quorum and backups
summary: etcd needs a majority of members. See how many failures a cluster survives and how much data a restore loses.

readouts.label: Data lost if you restore from backup

verdicts.text: Quorum is lost, so the cluster cannot commit writes. Running pods keep running, but nothing can change. Restore members or restore from a snapshot.
Still has quorum, but one more failure could break it. Replace the member now.
A single member has no failure tolerance. Use three or five.
All members are up.

tries: Use 3 members and take 2 down.
Use 5 members and take 2 down. Quorum holds.
Lengthen the backup interval and see the worst-case loss grow.

title: Node upgrade pace
summary: Upgrade nodes in batches. See how batch size changes duration and spare capacity, and when a disruption budget makes the upgrade wait.

inputs.label: A tight disruption budget protects the app

nodes.label: Batch
nodes.sub: b + " at a time, " + rounds + " rounds"

verdicts.text: The remaining nodes cannot carry the load while a batch is out. Pods go pending. Use a smaller batch or add temporary nodes.
A tight disruption budget will pause drains until pods are rescheduled elsewhere, so bigger batches may stall.
Little spare capacity during batches.
Batches finish quickly with capacity to spare.

tries: Upgrade 6 of 12 nodes at once at 60 percent load.
Drop to one at a time. Safe but slow.
Raise cluster load and see the safe batch size shrink.

title: Node loss and headroom
summary: When nodes drain or fail, their pods move to the rest. See how much spare capacity you need to survive N lost nodes.

readouts.label: Nodes worth of pods left pending
Highest safe utilisation for this loss

verdicts.text: After the loss the survivors cannot hold everything. Pods stay pending and the app loses capacity. Keep utilisation below the safe level, or add nodes.
The pods fit, but the nodes are nearly full, so little room for spikes.
The remaining nodes absorb the loss with room to spare.

tries: Run 90 percent busy and lose one node of 10.
Lower utilisation to the safe figure.
Lose a third of the nodes to simulate a zone.

title: RBAC blast radius
summary: If a pod token is stolen, what can the attacker reach? See how role scope and wildcard verbs change the damage.

inputs.label: Token is mounted in pods that do not need it

readouts.label: What they can do to them

verdicts.text: A cluster-wide role with every verb makes one stolen token a full compromise. Scope roles to a namespace and list only the verbs needed.
Every secret in the cluster is within reach. Prefer a namespace role.
Wildcard verbs let a thief change and delete, not only read.
Narrow scope and narrow verbs keep the damage small. Unmount tokens that pods do not need.

tries: Bind cluster-wide with wildcard verbs.
Change to namespace scope.
Untick the mounted token and see how the exposure drops.

title: Atomic upgrades and rollback
summary: A bad upgrade can leave a release half-broken. See how --atomic and waiting for readiness turn a failure into an automatic rollback.

inputs.label: Time for the new pods to become ready

verdicts.text: Without --wait the command reports success as soon as the manifests are applied. The broken pods roll out and nobody is told.
The command failed but the broken revision stays. Roll back by hand to the last good revision.
The failure triggered an automatic rollback, so the previous revision is serving again and the history shows it.
The upgrade succeeded and the new version is serving.

tries: Break the new version with neither flag.
Use --atomic.
Make pods ready later than the timeout.

title: Values precedence
summary: The same setting can come from the chart, a values file, or the command line. See which value wins as layers are added.
vars: set ? "--set" : (f2 ? "second values file" : (f1 ? "first values file" : "chart default"))

verdicts.text: --set beats every file. It is easy to forget, and it only lives in a shell history. Prefer values files in version control.
Later files override earlier ones, so the second file wins.
Only chart defaults or one file apply.

tries: Turn on both files, then add --set.
Remove --set. The later file wins.
Remove everything but the chart default.

title: Subchart version constraints
summary: A chart depends on a subchart at 1.2.0. See which version each constraint pulls in once newer releases appear, and how a lock file stops surprises.

verdicts.text: Caret takes new minors. A rebuild next month can deploy a different subchart than you tested. Commit the lock file.
Patch updates float in. They are usually safe, but you did not test them.
The version is pinned, so every build deploys what you tested.

tries: Use caret with newer minors and no lock.
Commit the lock file.
Use an exact constraint.

title: Helm upgrade and manual edits
summary: Someone edits a live resource with kubectl. See which changes a later helm upgrade keeps and which it overwrites.

inputs.label: The chart now sets a different replicas value
The chart sets replicas, but the same as last revision

readouts.label: Hand edit kept silently
readouts.expr: drift ? "yes, and now it differs from the chart" : "no"

verdicts.text: The chart did not change this field between revisions, so the live edit survives. The cluster now differs from what the chart says. Change values in version control instead.
The chart changed the field, so the hand edit is overwritten, and anyone who relied on it is surprised.
Nothing was edited by hand. The release matches the chart.

tries: Edit by hand and upgrade without changing the field.
Change the field in the chart too.
Leave both off.

title: Sync, self-heal and prune
summary: Git says one thing and the cluster another. See what Argo CD does about a hand edit and a deleted manifest under each sync policy.

inputs.label: A manifest was removed from git

readouts.label: Hand edit
readouts.expr: edit ? (fixed ? "reverted to git" : "stays, shown as out of sync") : "none"

readouts.label: Removed manifest
readouts.expr: removed ? (gone ? "deleted from the cluster" : "left running as an orphan") : "none"

verdicts.text: The resource was removed from git but pruning is off, so it keeps running and costs money. Turn on prune, or delete it by hand.
The edit stays until someone syncs. With self-heal on, it would be reverted.
Self-heal put the cluster back to what git says.
The cluster matches git.

tries: Edit a live resource with auto sync and self-heal on.
Turn self-heal off.
Remove a manifest with prune off.

title: Sync waves and ordering
summary: Resources sync wave by wave, and each wave must be healthy before the next starts. See total time and what a slow resource costs.

inputs.label: Time for a typical resource to be healthy
Wave that holds the slowest resource

verdicts.text: Ordered waves with a slow resource make syncs take minutes. Use waves only where order truly matters.
Ordering costs a minute or more per sync.
Ordering is cheap here.

tries: Add 6 waves with a slow resource.
Cut waves to 1.
Make the slow resource slower.

title: Git to cluster delay
summary: Argo CD polls git. See how long a merged change waits before it reaches the cluster, and how a webhook shortens that.

nodes.label: Argo CD
nodes.sub: hook ? 'notified at once' : 'polls every ' + poll + ' s'

readouts.label: Load on the git host
readouts.expr: hook ? "low" : fmt(60 / poll, 2) + " fetches per minute per app"

verdicts.text: A change can wait ten minutes before it starts. Add a webhook, or shorten the interval.
Polling is simple and robust. A webhook cuts the delay, and polling remains as a fallback.
Changes reach the cluster in seconds.

tries: Set the polling interval to 15 minutes.
Turn on the webhook.
Shorten polling and see the git load grow.

title: ApplicationSet fan-out
summary: One template generates an application for each cluster and service. See how the count grows and what that means for refresh load.

verdicts.text: Thousands of apps refreshing often put real load on the repo server and the git host. Lengthen the interval, use webhooks, or shard controllers.
Large fan-out. A bad template change now touches hundreds of applications at once, so roll it out gradually.
Manageable scale.

tries: Raise clusters and services to the top.
Lengthen the refresh interval.
Note how one template mistake multiplies.
